title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
primary_service: AWS machine learning and generative AI
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of retrieval-augmented generation and its relationship to AWS Machine Learning, AI, and Generative AI.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to retrieval-augmented generation.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn retrieval-augmented generation in the context of AWS Machine Learning, AI, and Generative AI. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Retrieval-Augmented Generation matters because it is one part of aws machine learning and generative ai. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Retrieval-Augmented Generation belongs to AWS Machine Learning, AI, and Generative AI. AI solutions require workload-appropriate model selection, scoped data access, retrieval quality, grounding, output validation, safety evaluation, monitoring and cost controls.

The PDF lists these subtopics: Embeddings and semantic search; Vector stores; Retrieval and grounding; Evaluating retrieval quality. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For retrieval-augmented generation, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: Embeddings and semantic search
items.text: Identify the AWS resource or design decision involved, the permissions and prerequisites it needs, and the evidence that shows it is configured as intended.

items.title: Vector stores
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: Retrieval and grounding
items.text: Define the input/data permissions, expected evidence, evaluation cases, safety boundaries and cost limits. A generated answer or completed invocation is not by itself proof of correctness.

content_blocks.title: Retrieval-augmented generation data path
content_blocks.code: Question → authorize caller → retrieve allowed documents → rank evidence → generate draft answer → validate citations and policy → return with traceable sources
content_blocks.expected_output: RAG reduces some unsupported answers by adding retrieved context, but it does not guarantee correctness or replace authorization/evaluation.

content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Retrieval-Augmented Generation”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Retrieval-Augmented Generation with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is taught as part of AWS Machine Learning, AI, and Generative AI.
AI solutions require workload-appropriate model selection, scoped data access, retrieval quality, grounding, output validation, safety evaluation, monitoring and cost controls.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
